en: Guhyāvalī: Om, homage to Vajrayoginī!
Just as copper does not turn into gold for living beings, even by means of great afflictions.
Even through service to the lotus of wisdom, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is not attained;
therefore, those who possess bodies formed from a mass of merit are merely partial in some respect.
Salutations to those Siddhas whose minds are like the billowing waves of the ocean of *nirmudrā*. ||1||

That consciousness which was described by the Blessed One through the union of the vajra and the lotus—where is it among sentient beings? Furthermore, in the process of the transmission of the tradition, supreme detachment arises from passion; this occurs through the instruction on thorough knowledge situated between the two joys.
For them, the state of liberation through the mudrās and other means was accomplished by means of the bliss of sexual union. ||2||

In that regard, first, he who— having abandoned the pleasure of women at the middle moment of the *virama* (cessation), which is free from passion for all other states— is absorbed in that other, immutable (*akṣara*) bliss, is the illustrious one,
skilled in the procedure of sealing with camphor by the command of the Guru.
The wise person, whose mind is reeling from drinking the nectar of one's own bliss, does not fall into delusion. ||3||
What talk can there be of those whose intellects are accustomed to moving through herds of cattle according to the rules of logic?
They direct their thunderbolt-strokes at the desert; for from this very foundation, they have acquired such impetuosity through the grace of the Guru’s feet.
For the accomplished one, attachment to wisdom itself becomes the unsurpassed state.
The Guru draws the mind away from its own substrate (svādhiṣṭhāna) for those possessed of intelligence,
and instantly produces that self-realized knowledge which is otherwise difficult to attain;
like a sun-crystal, it suddenly blazes forth when touched by the fuel of the meeting [of conditions].
The intrinsic nature of things cannot, by any means, be transcended through conjunction. ||5||
Whatever little we have attained on the various fragile paths has been spoken from our own limited knowledge; therefore, O wise ones, there is no fault here for which you should find reproach.
Thus, if through the application of wisdom there arises a further realization, [it is well].
Nor is there a third object [of knowledge] other than the Guru and one’s own self-abiding state (svādhiṣṭhāna). ||6||

At the end of passion, at the moment of entering the state of cessation, when the moon is established in its own nature, there arises the experience of the mind, the activity of which is stilled and the course of the breath is obstructed;
at that time, that bliss which cannot arise from anything else is the supreme state directly realized.
In that regard, he who possesses direct personal experience is indeed accomplished through Mahāmudrā. ||7||
Without the yoga of wisdom, he instantly brings about the state of the Vajra for the virtuous; or, through that yoga, by acting as an awakener like the cool-rayed moon—
he who knows the empowerment is the Guru here, and no other.
The power of such a person quickly overcomes even a wicked mind. ||8||
The moment born between the two joys is so extremely subtle that it is not perceived;
how then can one, at that time, effect [the union] through the mind by means of the yoga of the vajra and lotus?
Therefore, the virtuous diligently rely upon the imperishable bliss alone.
Having remained there for a long time with their minds composed, people again grasp the ultimate reality. ||9||
Is the water of the mirage to be grasped, like the throbbing of a tortoise’s eye,
by those who have heard the yoga of the lotus-born Brahmā in order to realize it directly in an instant?
That state of experience arises only from remaining for a long time.
When the moon has departed from the vajra, there is indeed no pleasure whatsoever here again. ||10||
If that very same absolute bliss which was previously attained through union with the beloved is now present, what further need is there for the attainment of the supreme seal (*mudrā*)?
Herein lies something else entirely different from the objects of external sensory pleasure.
Then, another certain one arises, the innate bliss Śambhu. ||11||
From the Guru’s own abode (svādhiṣṭhāna), the dissolution of the senses occurs for the wise; through that dissolution, pure consciousness alone flashes forth, independent within the three worlds.
What further extraordinary and supreme reality could there be beyond this? It is not soon attained.
Those by whom it was promised possess bodies that correspond to their trembling lips.
Even in a deity who has been produced through meritorious deeds and consecrated with auspicious rites,
there is a certain power that makes manifest what is placed within;
for a man who is a master of yoga yet resembles a beast, this occurs due to the absence of such power.
Even a deity, though hollow within, may have a body fashioned from soft and heavy stone. ||13||

That which is performed in a state where the goal has not been attained due to lack of practice, where the path is not mastered, where there is no instruction, and which occurs suddenly, effortlessly, constantly, through direct perception, and instantaneously— indeed, that which is done when one has desisted from the stage [of worldly activity] out of the bliss of the Guru’s command; [This verse is part of a larger work on the nature of spiritual realization.]
And that which becomes mere consciousness is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). ||14||
In this world, through yogas born from the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*),
this [yogi] does not abandon that which is to be enjoyed by the senses, which is like its own natural liberation;
yet he is one who has taken up the unceasing mental fluctuations of passion and the like, being a connoisseur of them.
One does not enter the goddess of self-awareness, just as one cannot reach the bottom of the water. ||15||
Those who relish these five vices fall into the dark well of sin; if not, they attain liberation by having their feet firmly established upon the ground of their own innate nature.
Otherwise, how could one enter that state of certainty through the pride of being free from conceptual construction?
He dwells within the ocean of saṃsāra; who else, then, could reach its further shore? 16.
These five lead one to the further shore of the river of delusion like a supreme boat; yet there is one other great obstacle to the remover of calamities:
the mind, intoxicated by the drinking of wine that is the beautiful attachment to the senses.
This elephant of fragrance, with its scent overflowing, is rushing toward this earth in the world. ||17||
Even in the company of women, liquor brings a man to the state of a eunuch; yet, once taken, it is not abandoned here by one whose intellect is so ordained.
For how can that which alone grants the pleasure of color to the five [senses]—as seen through experience—be anything other than this?
The second is that which pervades the entire world, both the stable and the moving. ||18||
Through an intellect rendered venerable by the lineage of succession from the Guru,
that very substratum— the speech of oneself and others— is extinguished;
for as one lamp is kindled from another, so too do others arise from it.
Lamps are produced here in succession; what wonder is there in this? ||19||
Just as one who is dull-witted and worships a blue flame that burns incessantly in an empty house finds happiness therein,
so too does he whose head is adorned by hundreds of prostrations at the lotus feet of the Guru [attain bliss].
Having obtained the streak of dust, he immediately attains the state of a Vajra-being. ||20||
Whether the Guru is near or far, what does it matter? For a child, how can there be the sudden attainment of realization across hundreds of leagues?
In the expanse of the sky, the sun [shines] for both of us...
The lotus blooms and the power of the mighty unfolds; is this anything to be wondered at? ||21||

Knowledge of reality is twofold: that which is with words and that which is inexpressible; one proceeds from the limbs [of yoga] and the other proceeds from the bodiless [direct experience]. That which, through constant awakening, prevails in the unity of these two— [This is the knowledge of reality.]
This very [Self] is established by itself as the supreme state beyond the path of the divisible lower [levels]. ||22||
Living beings are Vajradharas, and the women of the world are equal to the skull-bearing consorts;
I am this Heruka-form, in whom the Blessed One is present in his various vehicles.
Just as one who, out of reverence, partakes of the glorious lotus, the intoxicant, and the cow’s dung-fire—
The lord of yogis accomplishes all this with a mind that is one-pointed and beyond the senses. ||23||
In some cases through the application of wisdom, in others through the power of the five senses, in some through self-consecration, and in others through the path of the guru’s word;
according to the diversity of inclination in men, he whose hands are marked with the vajra makes [the truth] manifest.
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by it, for its state is beyond the reach of words.
O wise ones, let there be for me no study of the scriptures of truth here, nor let there be for me knowledge of the words and their meanings;
if only this [devotion] exists, arising from love for the dust of the lotus feet of the One who bears the wheel-mark.
The Guhyāvalī flashes forth; what, then, shall I do? ||25||
Thus ends the Guhyāvalī composed by Dauḍīpāda.
